query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of yttrium (Y) and hafnium (Hf) to refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) can improve their mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with a high melting point and superior mechanical strength at high temperatures
generation.intervention: Addition of a small amount of yttrium (Y) and hafnium (Hf) to RHEAs
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable solid solution with improved engineering characteristics
generation.mechanism: The addition of Y and Hf can enhance the high-temperature oxidation resistance and thermal stability of RHEAs, leading to improved mechanical performance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical performance, including strength and ductility, while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability
generation.baseline: RHEAs without the addition of Y and Hf
generation.boundary: The optimal ratio of alloy components and the amount of Y and Hf added
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of how Y and Hf improve the mechanical performance of RHEAs, and the potential trade-offs between mechanical and thermal properties

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare RHEA samples with and without the addition of Y and Hf, and subject them to high-temperature and irradiation tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Y and Hf does not improve the mechanical performance of RHEAs, or if it compromises their thermal and irradiation stability, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Especially in high-temperature applications, the microstructure of EHEA, with FCC+BCC phases, exhibits characteristics that are similar to the γ′ phase of nickel-based alloys, which has demonstrated outstanding resistance to oxidation [,]. Moreover, the unique eutectic solidification structure of EHEA provides a lower phase interface energy, and the significant sluggish diffusion effects characteristic of high-entropy alloys show its superior stability at higher temperatures [,]. Therefore, EHEA has great potential as a high-temperature protective coating. On the other hand, exploration of the properties of alloying elements and rare earth elements for high-entropy alloys has also never stopped [,,,]. Research about the effect of alloying elements on the performance of HEAs has predominantly concentrated on the mechanical properties while the literature indicates that conventional and high-entropy alloys and Y and Hf co-doping can effectively enhance the high-temperature oxidation resistance of alloys [,,]. In high-temperature corrosive environments, the stability and hot corrosion resistance performance of HEA coatings is the most significant field of concern. Given this backgroun

Therefore, in order to investigate the high-temperature protective capabilities of EHEA coatings, AlCoCrFeNi2.1 and AlCoCrFeNi2.1 co-doping with Y and Hf (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding in this paper. After their preparation, the microstructure and high-temperature thermal stability of the coatings were characterized, and the hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% (wt.%) NaCl mixed molten salt was investigated, which provided data support for an evaluation of the potential applications of high-entropy alloy coatings in harsh service environments such as steam pipelines and the hot-end components of gas turbines.
